Sarcoidosis: The patient's symptoms, including persistent dry cough, intermittent low-grade fever, night sweats, fatigue, weakness, and exertional shortness of breath, are consistent with sarcoidosis. The presence of nodular infiltrates in the bilateral upper lobes of the lungs and peri-hilar fullness on chest radiograph, as well as extensive bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with areas of perihilar and peripheral consolidation on CT scan, are also characteristic of sarcoidosis. The open lung biopsy showing sharply demarcated patchy fibrosed areas with fibrotic plugs and lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and foamy macrophages further supports this diagnosis. In contrast, the diagnostic differences between sarcoidosis and pulmonary hypertension, such as the presence of granulomas on biopsy and elevated pulmonary artery pressure, and between sarcoidosis and COVID-19 pneumonia, such as lymphopenia, elevated D-dimers, and ground-glass opacities on CT scan, help to distinguish sarcoidosis from these other conditions.
Pulmonary Hypertension: The patient's history of hypertension and the presence of exertional shortness of breath and fatigue are consistent with pulmonary hypertension. The CT scan showing extensive bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with areas of perihilar and peripheral consolidation could also be seen in pulmonary hypertension. However, the absence of right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary vascular resistance on the provided laboratory data, as well as the presence of granulomas on biopsy, which is more characteristic of sarcoidosis, make pulmonary hypertension a less likely diagnosis. The diagnostic differences between pulmonary hypertension and COVID-19 pneumonia, such as right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary vascular resistance, also help to distinguish pulmonary hypertension from COVID-19 pneumonia.
